analysis.one_liner: Requires 100% renewable electricity by 2035 and net-zero U.S. emissions by 2050.
analysis.headline: The Climate Solutions Act was introduced in November 2025 with no cosponsors and has been waiting in the Energy and Commerce Committee since the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Department of Energy to write rules so that 100% of U.S. retail electricity comes from renewable sources by 2035, and so that electricity and gas suppliers deliver rising amounts of energy savings to customers through 2032. It would also require the EPA to set annual emissions targets cutting U.S. greenhouse gas emissions at least 52% below 2005 levels by 2035 and to zero by 2050, with rules to enforce them. Suppliers could trade credits to meet their obligations, and states could still go further on their own.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that use electricity, especially in states where renewables are already cheaper to build than new fossil plants; people in communities hit hardest by extreme heat, wildfire smoke, and flooding; and the growing renewable energy and energy-efficiency industries, which would gain a guaranteed market as utilities race to meet the 100% renewable requirement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Electricity customers and clean energy firms

how_it_helps.text: Requires 100% of electricity sold at retail in the U.S. to be generated from renewable sources by 2035, with the share rising each year starting in 2026 [S3].

Sets escalating efficiency targets so electricity and gas suppliers must deliver growing annual savings to customers through 2032, which the bill's findings say can save consumers money on their bills [S3].

Directs the EPA to set binding emissions targets of at least 52% below 2005 levels by 2035 and zero net emissions by 2050, with implementing regulations due within seven years of enactment and five-year reviews after that [S2] [S3].
Lets suppliers meet efficiency targets through a market-based trading system and leaves state climate laws untouched, so states can still act independently [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal producers and the utilities that sell fossil power would see demand for their product fall as the 100% renewable requirement kicks in; some transition costs, such as grid upgrades and replacement generation, could show up in electricity rates during the build-out. Taxpayers would fund the National Academies reviews and federal rulemaking.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and their utilities

drawbacks.text: The 100% renewable electricity deadline of 2035 is only about ten years away and would require replacing nearly all fossil generation on the grid, a pace critics of similar proposals call unrealistic without vastly expanded transmission, storage, and permitting reform [S3].

The bill relies entirely on regulation rather than spending or incentives, and the costs of building replacement generation would be recovered through utility rates, so the timing and size of any bill savings for households are uncertain [S3].
The bill sets targets but leaves the details to future federal rulemaking, so the actual burden on any utility, plant, or household depends on regulations not yet written [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims at the largest single driver of U.S. emissions — the power sector — and pairs it with customer-savings mandates that could lower bills over time, but it asks for an enormous amount of grid change in a short window and provides no transition aid for workers and communities dependent on fossil fuel jobs. Whether households come out ahead depends heavily on rules and markets that do not yet exist. The bill's lack of cosponsors means none of these tradeoffs have been publicly tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on November 18, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on November 18, 2025 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day and no further action has been taken [S5].
No other member has signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has been forced to change anything: fossil fuel producers and utilities continue operating under current rules while the bill waits in committee.

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House and it was referred to committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no member of either party has cosponsored the bill, so no support has been tested in either chamber [S4].

industries.note: A 100% renewable electricity requirement and net-zero emissions targets would steadily shrink demand for fossil fuels used in power generation. The industry's current revenue depends on the fuels the bill phases out.

industries.industry: Renewable energy developers and equipment makers
industries.note: The bill creates a guaranteed, rising market for renewable generation as utilities must reach 100% renewables by 2035. Meeting that demand means construction and generation jobs in wind, solar, and storage.

Utilities would face mandatory efficiency savings targets and must shift their generation mix, but they can trade credits in a market-based system to comply, and efficiency programs can lower customer bills. The transition's cost recovery through rates is the open question.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee activity since referral, the realistic path is that the bill stays in committee for the rest of the Congress unless the sponsor builds a coalition. Most bills referred to House committees never receive a hearing or a vote.
